title: Diagnose and recover an application/schema migration mismatch
trigger: A customer path fails after a database change while PostgreSQL connectivity or service readiness remains healthy.
preconditions: identify the exact database change and deployed application version
confirm the failing customer path independently of health/readiness probes
capture the current schema and application error before changing either layer
run the version-controlled schema contract when available
determine whether the migration transformed, deleted, or only renamed metadata
obtain the required simulated change/rollback approval
diagnostic_steps: compare /health/ready with the affected customer endpoint
verify PostgreSQL reachability with a minimal SELECT 1
run db/schema-contract.sql and retain the failure output
inspect information_schema for missing, renamed, or type-changed columns
inspect application logs for SQLSTATE/missing-column/type errors
compare pre-change and current row counts and data fingerprints when a rollback is being considered
review whether the currently deployed application can support the migrated schema or requires a roll-forward release
mitigation_steps: use rollback only when the reverse change is proven safe and approved
for this DB-005 exercise, rename job_state back to processing_status only after the ticket fingerprint matches baseline
do not restart PostgreSQL for a schema-contract mismatch
do not execute an automatic reverse migration after destructive or data-transforming DDL
prefer roll-forward or DBA/development escalation when rollback would risk data loss or semantic corruption
validation_steps: the affected customer endpoint returns the expected success status
expected schema names/types are restored or the new application/schema pair is proven compatible
row count and data fingerprint match the approved recovery expectation
retain migration, application-log, schema, and recovery evidence for incident/change review
escalation_boundary: Escalate to DBA/development/change ownership when the migration transformed or dropped data, rollback SQL is not proven reversible, multiple application versions depend on different schema contracts, replication/backup implications exist, the schema contract cannot identify a safe target state, or a roll-forward application change is required.
